title: SpaceX's Starship: every test flight, from first launch to the first ship catch
dek: How the world's largest rocket went from losing both stages on its first flight in 2023 to being caught by its launch tower after almost a day in space, and what comes next.
seoTitle: SpaceX Starship test flights timeline: Flight 1 to 15
bigLabel: Starship test flights since April 2023: 10 counted as successes and 5 as failures, as of 14 November 2026

glance.what: Starship is SpaceX's giant two-stage rocket: a Super Heavy booster and the Starship spacecraft on top, both meant to be reused. On Flight 15 the spacecraft was caught by the arms of its launch tower in Texas after about 22.5 hours in space, the first time a rocket's upper stage has been recovered this way. The booster's catch was called off and it came down in the Gulf of Mexico.
glance.why: Reusing both stages, like an aircraft, could make launches much cheaper. Starship is central to SpaceX's next-generation Starlink satellites and to NASA's plan to land astronauts on the Moon.
glance.next: SpaceX is expected to try catching both stages on the next flight, and to begin launching from Florida. Mexico's environment agency is checking debris that washed up near the border after Flight 15; SpaceX says it found very little. Mexico wants talks with the US on Starship flights over its airspace. NASA's Moon plans need a demonstration of refuelling in orbit, planned for 2027.

forYou: Starship is how SpaceX plans to launch its next-generation Starlink internet satellites, which are bigger and faster than today's. If both stages can be caught and flown again quickly, the cost of getting things into space could fall sharply, which affects everything from satellite internet to Moon missions.
next: Flight 16: a likely attempt to catch both stages, and Starship's first launch from Florida; no date announced. Mexico is seeking US talks on Starship flights over its airspace and wants SpaceX to collect suspected debris; SpaceX says little was found.

events.title: Flight 1: clears the pad, then is lost
events.summary: The first full Starship launch. Several engines fail and both stages are lost over the Gulf of Mexico. SpaceX calls it a success because its main goal was to clear the launch pad.

events.title: Flight 2: both stages lost
events.summary: The booster is lost over the Gulf and the ship is destroyed by its flight termination system after a fire.

events.title: Flight 3: reaches space, lost on reentry
events.summary: Launch and stage separation succeed, but the booster is lost during its landing burn and the ship breaks up when it comes back into the atmosphere.

events.title: Flight 4: both stages splash down under control
events.summary: For the first time, both the booster and the ship make controlled splashdowns, the booster in the Gulf and the ship in the Indian Ocean.

events.title: Flight 5: the tower catches a booster
events.summary: The Super Heavy booster flies back to Starbase and is caught by the launch tower's "chopstick" arms, a first. The ship splashes down in the Indian Ocean.

events.title: Flight 6: booster diverted to the sea
events.summary: The booster catch is called off because of damage to the tower and it splashes down in the Gulf. The ship completes a controlled splashdown.

events.title: Flights 7 and 8: boosters caught, ships lost
events.summary: On both flights the booster is caught by the tower, but the ship is lost minutes into flight: after a propellant leak on Flight 7 (16 January) and after engines shut down on Flight 8 (6 March).

events.title: Flight 9: both stages lost
events.summary: The booster, flying for the second time, is lost before splashdown, and the ship fails to release its payload and breaks up over the Indian Ocean.

events.title: Flight 10: back on track
events.summary: Both stages complete controlled splashdowns, and the ship releases eight dummy Starlink satellites for the first time and relights an engine in space.

events.title: Flight 11: last flight of the second design
events.summary: Another success, with the ship landing on target in the Indian Ocean. It is the final flight of the "Block 2" version.

events.title: Flight 12: the bigger Block 3 debuts
events.summary: The first flight of the larger third-generation Starship, from a new launch pad. The ship splashes down under control, but the booster is lost after its landing burn fails.

events.title: Flight 13: first real Starlink satellites
events.summary: The ship releases 20 next-generation Starlink V3 satellites, the first working ones, on a path that brings them back down soon after, and returns intact. The booster is lost after engine failures.

events.title: Flight 14: first time in orbit
events.summary: Starship reaches orbit for the first time and places 26 Starlink V3 satellites in orbit, despite one upper-stage engine shutting down early. The flight is cut short and the ship splashes down in the Pacific.

events.title: Flight 15 launches; booster catch called off
events.summary: Flight 15 lifts off from Starbase, aiming to catch both stages for the first time. The booster's catch is aborted after a low-fuel alarm and it is sent to the Gulf of Mexico; CNBC reports it exploded before hitting the water. The ship reaches orbit and releases 26 more Starlink V3 satellites.

events.title: The tower catches the ship
events.summary: After about 22.5 hours in flight (around 14 orbits of Earth, according to CNBC), Ship 42 flies back to Starbase and is caught by the tower arms at 3:20 pm Texas time on 14 November, the first time a rocket's upper stage has returned from orbit to be caught for reuse. "We caught a Starship, and now everything changes," says SpaceX's Dan Huot.

events.title: Debris on a Mexican beach; SpaceX says it found very little
events.summary: Mexico's federal environment agency, Profepa, said debris began washing up on Playa Bagdad in Tamaulipas, just across the border from Starbase, on the morning of 17 November, after the Flight 15 booster came down in the Gulf of Mexico. Profepa said it would take custody of the material and ask SpaceX to take responsibility for anything traced to its launches. The conservation group Conibio reported plastic, tape and adhesive fragments offshore. On 19 November SpaceX said its teams found very few fragments, that their origin was not confirmed, and that social media claims of widespread damage were false or misleading. It cited independent tests finding no chemical, biological or toxicological risk in Starship's materials and offered to help if Mexican authorities ask. Investigators have not yet said which pieces came from Flight 15.
events.differs: Conibio, as reported by NeoTeo citing WIRED en Español, estimated 'thousands, possibly millions' of fragments; SpaceX says its teams found very few.

events.title: Mexico says SpaceX must take responsibility for suspected debris near Matamoros
events.summary: Mexican authorities said SpaceX must take responsibility for suspected rocket debris washing up on beaches near Matamoros, across the border from Starbase, per Texas Public Radio and the Texas Tribune. An environmental group, Conibio Global, says it has found at least 1,500 fragments that look like plastic, rubber and adhesive, and believes they came from the Flight 15 booster; it says this still needs confirming. A dead sea turtle is being examined. Mexico's environment agency, Profepa, told people not to touch fragments. SpaceX said on 19 November that its partners found "very little debris" and called claims of widespread damage "outright fabrications or intentionally misleading". No date has been announced for Flight 16.
events.status: Stated · Mexican authorities; Allegation · Conibio Global; SpaceX disputes

events.title: Mexico seeks talks with the US on Starship flights over its airspace
events.summary: Mexico's President Claudia Sheinbaum said her government will seek, through its embassy, a meeting between US and Mexican airspace authorities to set terms for Starship flights over Mexico, including how often they happen. She said the launch site could be moved "if necessary", and that the suspected debris near Matamoros is a separate issue. Mexico's navy is holding the debris, and its environment agency, Profepa, says it will ask SpaceX to collect it. SpaceX says it is working with Mexican authorities, that partners found "very little debris", and that what was found is "not clearly from SpaceX operations". SpaceX has asked US regulators to allow many more launches a year from Starbase.
events.status: Stated · President Sheinbaum; SpaceX disputes debris link
events.differs: Alto Nivel's headline says Sheinbaum will ask the US to relocate SpaceX's base; its report and Reuters both say she only did not rule out moving the launch site if necessary.
